abstract: Collective animal behavior is commonly explained by sensory-mediated interactions among individuals, yet physical interactions between moving bodies and their environment may also contribute to coordination. In fish schooling, passive hydrodynamic interactions have long been proposed to facilitate collective organization, but biological evidence remains limited because their effects are difficult to disentangle from active sensorimotor responses. Here, we combine computational simulations and physical experiments with self-propelled foils to identify balanced vortex interactions and develop a Vortex Balance Model (VBM) that predicts schooling configurations from swimming kinematics and relative tailbeat phase. We test these predictions using pairs of goldfish (Carassius auratus) swimming in a flow tank under three sensory conditions: intact vision and lateral-line sensing, visual deprivation with intact lateral-line sensing, and combined visual deprivation and reversible lateral-line impairment. Agreement between observed schooling configurations and VBM predictions increases as sensory input is reduced, reaching its highest level when both sensory modalities are impaired. These findings provide indirect biological evidence that passive hydrodynamic interactions contribute to fish schooling, while their effects can be modified or overridden by active sensorimotor responses.
